------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Today's Goals

- Introduce confidence intervals as a method for estimating a parameter

- Use bootstrapping as a means of creating confidence intervals



# Confidence Intervals


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Point Estimates

- To estimate a population parameter, we can use a sample statistic.
    - **Ex:**  You're hosting a pizza party for 200 people, and need to know what proportion [$p$]{style="color:red;"} of vegetarian pizza to order. 
    - **Idea:** Ask a (random) sample of attendees about their pizza preference and use the proportion [$\widehat{p}$]{style="color:red;"} in the sample as an estimate for the total proportion $p$.
  

- Your sample statistic, $\widehat{p}$, is a good guess for the population parameter.
  - **Terminology:** We sometimes call our sample statistic a [point estimate]{style="color:red;"}.
  


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Point Estimates vs. Interval Estimates

- A sample statistic is a good guess for the population parameter, but not the whole story
    - **Q:** After polling pizza party attendees, you find $\widehat{p} = 0.33$. What factor(s) determine your (un)certainty in this estimate?
  

- It may be preferable to estimate the proportion using **a range of values**, with smaller intervals corresponding to precision.
  - With just **$n = 9$** people, you might give a range of **$0.03$ to $0.63$** for $p$.
  
  - But with **$n = 48$**, you might instead give the range **$0.20$ to $0.46$**.



- We call these ranges **interval estimates**.


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Interval Estimates

::: fragment
A **confidence interval estimate** for a parameter *[usually]{.underline}* takes the form
$$
\textrm{Statistic }\pm \textrm{ Margin of Error (ME)}
$$
:::

::: fragment
The confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter.
:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}
  - e.g., when sampling pizza preferences with $n=48$, we estimate $p$ using the interval 
    
$$
   0.20 \textrm{ to } 0.46  \qquad \textrm{ or } \qquad \underbrace{0.33}_{\text{Statistic ($\widehat{p}$)}} \pm \ \ \ \underbrace{0.13}_{\text{ME}} 
$$

:::

::: fragment
The **Margin of Error** determines the width of the interval ($2*\text{Margin of Error}$)
:::

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}
  - e.g., in our pizza interval, the width is:
$$
   0.46 - 0.20 = 0.26 = 2 * \underbrace{0.13}_{\text{ME}}
$$

:::

**Q:** How should we choose our Margin of Error? (think *conceptually*)
 
 
------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals using the Sampling Distribution
 
- **Goal**: Figure out a reasonable **Margin of Error**

- In our example, suppose $p = 0.25$ (i.e., 25% of all party attendees prefer vegetarian)

- For approximately bell-shaped sampling distributions, **95\% of all sample statistics are within 2 SE of the parameter.**

::: fragment

```{r out.width = "70%", fig.height=2.5, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(1010)
n<-10000
p <- 0.25
sample_size <- 48
p_hat<-rbinom(n, size = sample_size, prob = p)/sample_size
se <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/sample_size)
dd<-data.frame(p_hat)

ggplot()+geom_histogram(data = dd, aes(x  = p_hat), binwidth = 1/sample_size, color = "white", fill = "gray60")+
  labs(x = "Sample Proportion", title = "Sampling Distribution, n = 48, True parameter: p = .25", y = NULL)+
  geom_rect(data =data.frame(x=0, y = 0), xmin = p-2*se, xmax =p+2*se, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "gray50", alpha = .3)+
 scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, by = .05))+
#  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL)+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = paste("2*SE =",2*se), x = p+2*se, y = 900)+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "p", color = "magenta3", x = p+.01, y = 1500, size = 4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = p, color = "magenta3") +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlim(c(0, 0.525))
```

:::

- This also means that **for 95\% of all samples, the [parameter]{.underline} will be within a distance of 2 SE of the sample [statistic]{.underline}** (every sample in the gray region) 


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Intervals
  
**Idea:** Build an interval centered at the sample statistic, with a margin of error of $2\cdot SE$:

$$
\widehat{p} \pm 2\cdot \textrm{SE}
$$
  
  
  - Intervals constructed this way will contain the parameter $p$ in 95% of samples!

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

```{r out.width = "70%", fig.height=2.5, echo=FALSE}
ggplot()+geom_histogram(data = dd, aes(x  = p_hat), binwidth = 1/sample_size, color = "white", fill = "gray60")+
  labs(x = "Sample Proportion", title = "Sampling Distribution, n = 48, True parameter: p = .25", y = NULL)+
  geom_rect(data =data.frame(x=0, y = 0), xmin = p-2*se, xmax =p+2*se, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "gray50", alpha = .3)+
 scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, by = .05))+
#  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL)+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = paste("2*SE =",2*se), x = p+2.25*se, y = 600)+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "p", color = "magenta3", x = p+.01, y = 1500, size = 4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = .33, color = "forestgreen")+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = expression(hat(p)), color = "forestgreen", x = .34, y = 1400, size = 4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = p, color = "magenta3")+
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33 + 2*se, y = 200, xend = .33, yend = 200), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "dodgerblue", lwd = 1)+
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33-2*se, y = 200, xend = .33, yend = 200), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "dodgerblue", lwd = 1)+
  annotate(geom = "point", x = .33, y = 200, color = "dodgerblue", size = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  xlim(c(0, 0.525))
```


- The interval for our sample was $0.33 \pm 0.125$, which *does* contain the parameter $p$

:::

## Another way to visualize this

::::: columns

::: {.column .nonincremental}

Imagine we...

- draw a sample from our population with $p = 40$
- calculate the sample statistic in that sample
- construct a confidence interval for that sample using $\widehat{p} \pm 2\cdot \textrm{SE}$

:::

::: column

```{r, fig.height = 8.25, fig.width = 5, echo=FALSE}
set.seed(111)

x <- data.frame(sample = 1:100, p = 40, phat = rnorm(100, 40, 2.5)) %>%
  mutate(lower = phat - 5, upper = phat + 5) %>%
  mutate(covers = p > lower & p < upper)

ggplot(x[51, ], aes(x = phat, y = sample)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = upper, xend = lower, y = sample, yend = sample, color = covers)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = p), lty = 2, lwd = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "gray30", "FALSE" = "magenta3"),
                     guide = "none") +
  xlab("Sample Statistic") + ylab("") +
  xlim(c(27, 53)) + ylim(c(0, 100)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "1 sample and its confidence interval",
       subtitle = "")

```

:::
:::::

## Confidence levels

- On the previous slide, 95\% of confidence intervals *across all samples* would contain the true parameter, $p$.

- Thus, we call each interval estimate a **95\% confidence interval**.
  

- Here, 95\% is our **confidence level**: The success rate for our estimation technique.
  - e.g., The pizza interval $0.33 \pm 0.13$ has confidence level of 95\%
  

- The confidence level corresponds to **the percentage of samples that would yield a corresponding confidence interval containing the true value of the parameter**.


::: fragment

```{r out.width = "70%", fig.height=2.5, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(x, aes(y = phat, x = sample)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(y = upper, yend = lower, x = sample, xend = sample, color = covers)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = p), lty = 2, lwd = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "gray30", "FALSE" = "magenta3"),
                     guide = "none") +
  ylab("Sample Statistic") + xlab("") +
  ylim(c(27, 53)) + xlim(c(0, 100)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "100 different samples and their confidence intervals",
       subtitle = "Confidence interval coverage: 94/100 = 94%")
```

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence levels

- **[Confidence Level:]{.underline}** the percentage of samples that would yield a corresponding confidence interval containing the true value of the parameter.


- For example, were we to:
    - Repeatedly draw samples from the population, and
    - Create 95\% confidence intervals in each sample...
    - 95\% of those confidence intervals would contain the true parameter



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recap: Confidence Intervals

- Confidence intervals consist of 1. **an interval estimate** and 2. **a confidence level**.

- In our pizza party sample, we estimated the true proportion of vegetarian pizza-eaters was between **$0.20$ and $0.46$**, with **$95\%$ confidence**.



- What does "95\% confidence" mean?
    - It's the success rate **[of the process]{.underline}**
    - For 95\% of all samples, the interval we construct will actually contain the parameter.


- Worth emphasizing: it's the success rate **of The Process, [NOT]{.underline} the specific interval you calculated in your sample.**
    - The parameter is either in your interval, or it's not -- there's no success rate there!


------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Think-Pair-Share



**Q:** What's the difference between these two interpretations of a 95\% confidence interval?

  - For 95\% of all samples, the interval we construct will actually contain the parameter.
  
  - For a given interval, there is a 95\% chance that the parameter will fall in the interval. 
  
  
```{r}
#| echo: false
countdown::countdown(3)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Think-Pair-Share (Answer) 



**Q:** What's the difference between these two interpretations of a 95\% confidence interval?

  - For 95\% of all samples, the interval we construct will actually contain the parameter.
  
  - For a given interval, there is a 95\% chance that the parameter will fall in the interval. 

<br>

::: fragment

**A:**

:::

- The first one is accurate! 95\% confidence refers to the accuracy of the *process*

- **The second one is wrong, an easy mistake to make!!** It confuses probability of the process with a deterministic outcome. Our sample statistic "moves" with sampling variability - the parameter does not.


------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Interval Width and Sample Size ($n$)
  
**Idea:** Build a 95\% confidence interval centered at the sample statistic, with a margin of error of $2\cdot SE$:
$$
\widehat{p} \pm \underbrace{2\cdot \textrm{SE}}_{\text{Margin of Error}}
$$



- This interval's **width is determined by the Standard Error (SE).**

- **Reminder:** The SE is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution.

- **Q:** What do we know about the SE as the sample size ($n$) increases?

- **Q:** What does this imply about the interval's width  as the sample size ($n$) increases?
    - The SE gets smaller as $n$ increases!
    - Our interval becomes narrower as $n$ increases!


------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Interval Width and Confidence Level

::: {style="font-size:0.9em;"}
  
**Idea:** Build an 95\% confidence interval centered at the sample statistic, with a margin of error of $2\cdot SE$:
$$
\widehat{p} \pm \underbrace{2\cdot \textrm{SE}}_{\text{Margin of Error}}
$$

- Chose $\text{Margin of Error} = 2*SE$ because 95\% of sample statistics fall within $2*SE$ of the parameter (in sampling distribution).


- **Fun Fact:** 9[0]{.underline}\% of sample statistics fall within $1.64*SE$ of the parameter.
    - **Q**: What would happen if we did the following interval?
$$
\widehat{p} \pm 1.64*\textrm{SE}
$$
    - We would get a 9[0]{.underline}\% confidence interval!
    - This interval is narrower, but **has a lower "success" rate!** For 9[0]{.underline}\% of all samples, the interval will contain the parameter.
    
:::


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Interval Width and Confidence Level

- **[Takeaway:]{.underline} The confidence level also determines the width of the interval!**
  
  - higher confidence (e.g., 95\%) means a *larger* margin of error (*wider* interval)
  
  - lower confidence (e.g., 90\%)  means a *smaller* margin of error (*narrower* interval)
  

```{r, echo = FALSE}
ggplot()+geom_histogram(data = dd, aes(x  = p_hat), binwidth = 1/sample_size, color = "white", fill = "gray60")+
  labs(x = "Sample Proportion", title = "Sampling Distribution, n = 48, True parameter: p = .25", y = NULL)+
  geom_rect(data =data.frame(x=0, y = 0), xmin = p-2*se, xmax =p+2*se, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "gray50", alpha = .2)+
 scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, .5, by = .05))+
#  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL)+
  annotate(geom = "text", label = "p", color = "magenta2", x = p+.01, y = 1500, size = 4)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = p, color = "magenta2", lwd = 1)+
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0.33), lty = 2) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33 + 2*se, y = 200, xend = .33, yend = 200), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "dodgerblue", lwd = 1)+
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33-2*se, y = 200, xend = .33, yend = 200), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "dodgerblue", lwd = 1)+
  annotate(geom = "point", x = .33, y = 200, color = "dodgerblue", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = .47, y = 200, label = " 95%", color = "dodgerblue") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33 + 1.64*se, y = 400, xend = .33, yend = 400), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "goldenrod", lwd = 1)+
  geom_segment(aes(x = .33-1.64*se, y = 400, xend = .33, yend = 400), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first", type = "closed"), color = "goldenrod", lwd = 1)+
  annotate(geom = "point", x = .33, y = 400, color = "goldenrod", size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = .45, y = 400, label = " 90%", color = "goldenrod") +
  theme_bw()
```



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Problems(?) with Confidence Intervals

Let's say we're working with 95\% confidence intervals



- **Problem 1:** We only have 1 sample, and we don't know if it belongs to the 95% of "good" samples, or the 5% of "bad" ones
    - **Consolation:** If I go through life constructing 95% confidence intervals, I will be right about 95% of the time 
    - That's not bad!
  
<br>

- **Problem 2:** To make a confidence interval, we need the sampling distribution in order to compute the standard error. But in practice, we (often) don't have direct access to this.
  - **Solution:** approximate the sampling distribution via bootstrapping!




# Bootstrap Confidence Intervals: Example in R


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Sleep for Reed Students

Suppose we wish to estimate **how many hours Reed students sleep, on average** with a sample of 50 students, who we surveys on hours of sleep.

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

```{r echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
library(gridExtra)
set.seed(10)
sleep <- data.frame(Student=1:50, Hours = 9 - rgamma(50, 2, 1))
ggplot(sleep, aes(x = Hours))+geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, color = "white")+
  labs(title = "Sample Distribution of Sleep at Reed College")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(sleep$Hours), color = "red", size = 1.5)+
  annotate("text", x = mean(sleep$Hours)-.15, y = 6.5, label = expression(bar(x)), color = "red", size = 10)
```

::: fragment

```{r echo = TRUE}
head(sleep, 4)
sleep %>% summarize(MeanSleep = round(mean(Hours), 3))
```

:::

:::

::: {.column width=50%}

- Is the true average hours of sleep at Reed is 7.046?
    - Surely not! This is just one sample of size 50
  

- Let's create a *confidence interval* for the true average hours 
    - We can **use the bootstrap distribution to estimate the SE** needed for the interval

:::
:::::
  
  
------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bootstrap Average Sleep


::::: columns
::: {.column width=36%}

Create the bootstrap samples: 

- **Q**: What is each argument of `rep_sample_n()` doing?

- Each bootstrap sample consists of 50 observations sampled *with replacement* from the original sample (`size = 50`)

- We have a total of 10,000 bootstrap samples (`reps = 10000`)

:::

::: {.column width=55%}

```{r echo = T, eval = F}
bootstrap_samples <- sleep %>% 
  rep_sample_n(size = 50, replace = TRUE, 
               reps = 10000)
bootstrap_samples
```
```{r echo = F, eval = T}
set.seed(121)
bootstrap_samples <- sleep %>% 
  rep_sample_n(size = 50, replace = TRUE, reps = 10000)
bootstrap_samples
```

:::
:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bootstrap Average Sleep

Compute bootstrap statistics: (Mean of each *bootstrap* sample)

::::: columns

::: {.column width=50%}

```{r echo = T}
bootstrap_stats <- bootstrap_samples %>% 
  group_by(replicate) %>% 
  summarize(x_bar = mean(Hours))
```



```{r echo = T}
bootstrap_stats
```


:::

::: {.column width=50%}


- We now have 10,000 sample means based on the bootstrap samples, and can assess their variability

:::

:::::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bootstrap Average Sleep


Graph the bootstrap distribution:

```{r fig.height=2.5, fig.width = 6 , echo = F}
ggplot(bootstrap_stats, aes(x = x_bar))+
  geom_histogram(bins = 34, color = "white")+
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution for Average Sleep, n = 50", x = expression(bar(x)))
```


- Use the bootstrap distribution to **estimate** the standard error:

::: fragment
```{r echo = F}
r0_se <- bootstrap_stats %>% summarize(SE = sd(x_bar)) %>% pull()
```

```{r echo = T}
bootstrap_stats %>% summarize(SE = sd(x_bar))
# or equivalently
sd(bootstrap_stats$x_bar)
```

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Confidence Interval for Average Sleep

- Our sample average sleep was **$\bar x = 7.046$.**



- Based on the bootstrap distribution, this statistic has [Standard Error=`r round(r0_se,3)`]{style="color:blue;"}.



- Our 95% confidence interval for the true average hours of sleep for Reed students is:
$$
{7.046} \pm 2 \cdot \color{blue}{0.165} 
$$


::: {.fragment .center}

```{r}
se_hat <- sd(bootstrap_stats$x_bar)
c(7.046 - 2 * se_hat, 7.046 + 2 * se_hat)
```

:::

  - Our best guess for average nightly sleep is that it's between `r 7.046 - 2*round(r0_se,3)` and `r 7.046 + 2*round(r0_se,3)`. This method has a success rate of $95\%$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Bootstrap Confidence Intervals: Complete Code Example

::: {style="font-size:0.9em;"}
We are given the data frame `sleep`. Our [statistic of interest is the average hours of sleep per night in the sample]{.underline} contained in this data frame (recorded individually as `Hours`). We can use the **bootstrap method** to calculate confidence intervals for the [parameter, the average hours of sleep per night in the population]{.underline}: 
:::

<br>

```{r eval = F}
set.seed(121)
sleep <- read.csv("data-path.csv")  # Read in the data

bootstrap_samples <- sleep %>%   # Creating our 10,000 bootstrap samples
  rep_sample_n(size = 50, replace = TRUE, reps = 10000)

bootstrap_stats <- bootstrap_samples %>%  # Calculating bootstrap statistics
  group_by(replicate) %>%                 # from each sample.
  summarize(x_bar = mean(Hours))

ggplot(bootstrap_stats, aes(x = x_bar))+  # Graph the bootstrap distribution
  geom_histogram(bins = 34, color = "white")+
  labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution for Average Sleep, n = 50", x = expression(bar(x)))

se_hat <- sd(bootstrap_stats$x_bar)  # Estimate the standard error
xbar <- mean(sleep$Hours)  # This is our **statistic**, 7.046
c(xbar - 2 * se_hat, xbar + 2 * se_hat)  # Calculate confidence interval
```
